title: GPS clocks gain 38 microseconds a day

yt.title: GPS clocks run 38.5 microseconds fast every day #Shorts
yt.description:
Weak-field approximations: gravitational term GM/c^2 x (1/R_earth - 1/r_orbit), velocity term v^2/(2c^2), with GM = 3.986004418e14 m^3/s^2 (WGS 84), mean Earth radius 6,371 km, GPS orbit radius about 26,560 km, c = 299,792,458 m/s. Per day: +45.7 - 7.2 = 38.5 microseconds. Light covers about 11.5 km in that time. GPS satellite clocks are set to a slightly lower frequency before launch to compensate (N. Ashby, "Relativity in the Global Positioning System", Living Reviews in Relativity, 2003).
Narration is AI-generated.

scenes.narration: The clocks on GPS satellites do not tick at the same rate as clocks on the ground.
Up there, gravity is weaker, so their clocks run faster, by about forty-five point seven microseconds a day. But they also move fast, which slows them by about seven point two.

scenes.label: gained per day by a GPS clock
scenes.narration: Net, each satellite clock gains about thirty-eight point five microseconds every day. We computed it from Einstein's formulas.
In that time, light travels about eleven point five kilometers. Left uncorrected, positions would drift by kilometers every day, so engineers tune the satellite clocks before launch.
